unplaced.en: The editor comments on the Greek phrase 'having a motion toward some cause': this chiefly concerns the cause that is the end toward which a thing moves, since it exists from that cause as from an efficient cause. Picus did not express it well in saying 'it is referred to no cause at all', since a thing is also said to be referred to a cause when it traces its origin to it in some way, even if it is not moved toward it; as in the Godhead the Son is referred to the Father as to the cause (as the Greeks are accustomed to say), yet he is not moved toward him, nor has motion, as toward a cause in the sense of an end, in the way Catholics speak of any of them: for he is not so for the sake of an end, but with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the one end of all, as there is one goodness, as there is one nature. Hence he is called by Gregory the Theologian and by Maximus 'without cause' (anaitios), having no cause or end, in so far as he is for himself, but 'through a cause' (di' aitian), on account of the cause, in so far as he became man for our sake. One must therefore speak with more care in theology, lest any obscurity, still less any error, creep into the theology of Maximus, the most careful of theologians.

Scite vero Maximus ex discretis seu notionalibus in Deo, probat conjuncta et essentialia: Verbum scilicet mente præditum, quod a Mente essentialiter subsistente (Patre scilicet) nascendo esse habeat; idemque vivere, quod Vitæ essentialiter subsistenti, Spiritui sancto, coexsistat.

The editor reports that earlier editions lacked the word synuparchousan (co-existing), without which Maximus's chapter was truly obscure, as if that participle referred back to the participle placed above; and it might then be said that Life, so subsisting, begets the Word or does something else for him, whereas he rather receives from him, from whom Life also proceeds, together with the Father, as from one principle, as the catholic faith teaches. Maximus argues skilfully from the distinct, or notional, features in God to the joint and essential ones: the Word, endowed with mind, has his being by birth from the Mind subsisting essentially (the Father), and likewise lives because he co-exists with the Life subsisting essentially, the Holy Spirit.

unplaced.en: On the words 'sole father, in his essence, of the sole unoriginate Word.' The Greek word anarchos is ambiguous: it can mean existence from eternity before all duration, and also having no origin from another. So Gregory the Theologian in his theological works rightly allows the Son and Word to be 'without beginning' in the first sense and rightly denies it in the second, so that the monarchy and unity of the blessed Trinity stand clear. The editor therefore finds Picus's gloss, 'sole begetter of the Word who has no origin, according to substance', poor: it seems self-contradictory and to deny the Word's birth, which Picus himself asserts; for who, and how, is a begetter whose begetting is wholly without origin, since birth and being begotten are themselves the origin or procession of a living thing from a living thing joined to it? One should not treat theology so loosely, if one is no theologian. As for what Maximus says of the Holy Spirit, it is common to all the Greeks, who nevertheless take care to add the exclusive term 'only' to the procession of the Word from the principle, never to the procession of the Spirit, so that there is no discord of ours; the long-standing Greek discord, which later strife of minds introduced, arose when others objected to what the Greeks allowed themselves to add for explanation. unplaced.en: On 'the impassibility (dyspatheia) of the saints.' The editor explains that Maximus means that, in the struggle of vice and virtue, those who are earnestly devoted to virtue are as if hardened, so that they cannot easily be harmed by vice; this is the force of the word as Maximus uses it here, and examples of that sense are found in Budaeus and Henri Estienne. What Picus gives, 'the conflict of the affections that is in the saints', is beside the point, since the word does not bear that sense; it could be rendered 'trouble, toil' (as in chapters 19 and 21), but that suits Maximus's purpose here less well. The editor also says Picus wrongly renders the final clause of the chapter ('that he may hold the good, even in misfortunes having the advantage'), as if it meant 'that he may keep the good and the richer in calamities'; Maximus fully intends to keep the upright in their duty, whose lot even in hardships is the better one, or who rejoice, grown strong in virtue and Christian fortitude, the most blessed of all and having the advantage over all adversaries. The editor suggests the gospel promise (a hundredfold 'now in this time, with persecutions', Mark x, 30), which Maximus states well in saying that those who do right are punished and afflicted because they cultivate virtue and hold to duty; and Maximus explains the matter further in the next chapter, whose last line is a golden saying: 'strength of soul for those who endure: the scourging of the body.' (This quoted saying is rendered in the note itself as 'robur animi per patientiam, injuria ac sugillatio corporis'.) The note also includes a French phrase, 'Qui ont l'avantage même dans les afflictions', cited from a translation.

unplaced.en: On 'through the one and unchanging will.' The editor objects that Picus renders the Greek word 'aparallakton' as 'unchangeable', and soon after, in chapter 29, in the phrase 'the deified man's aparallaxia towards God in respect of the good', as 'the impossible separation of the deified from God'; this is far from the truth and from sound doctrine. In both places 'aparallakton' and 'aparallaxia' mean exact likeness, with almost no difference or variation (Hesychius). The editor says what Philoxenus and the old Glossary of Estienne meant, when they explain it as 'indiscrete', and quotes Gregory (Christmas oration), 'the image in all things alike'. Theologians use this sense constantly, whether of the divine persons or of those in whom, so far as is granted to man, likeness to God is perfect by charity, which yet makes neither an unchangeable state nor an impossible separation from God, setting aside the final consummation and the vision of God, which Maximus is not discussing here. Picus may have been misled by Estienne's Thesaurus index, where, without naming an author, the word is glossed 'not to change, or immutability, constancy', although the same work (vol. 1) explains it well; and Bilibaldus is said to argue, on the Gregory passage, that it was wrongly rendered 'unchangeable likeness'. unplaced.en: On 'they would contribute to the definition of nature.' The editor takes it as 'would be contributed', and as he has rendered more commonly and plainly, 'would look to, would belong to, the definition of nature.' Picus's 'for they would also have contributed to the end' is not good: horos (definition) is one thing, end another, although horos also means a boundary, which is the definition itself. The note breaks off at 'Etiam to' and continues at the head of the foot block on the next page. Continuation of note (q) from the previous page, here on 'proegoumenos'. The editor says 'ab initio' (from the beginning) is not a good rendering; it means 'first, or primarily', that is, by first destination, as if God in creating man had intended to equip him with these. Maximus, with Nyssa, denies it; it is quite true of the affections as they are truly 'pathe', or perturbations, which smack of vice and are not perfectly subject to reason. Yet they do belong to the definition of man, not under the formal aspect of man but as he also exists as an animal; for man is not pure soul and mind, unless we wish to think as Origen did. Maximus and other Fathers everywhere maintain that these energies were necessary in Christ, so that the truth of human nature might be shown in him. Just as Adam and Eve, before whom we blush when naked, were naked and did not blush, because they felt no rebellious motion in themselves; and thus their bodies too had been made 'proegoumenos'; so also the passions, the affections of the sentient powers, and the energies, each in proportion as it was disposed toward its end and object, but with the greatest tranquillity and without disturbance or trouble.

unplaced.en: On 'having completely passed beyond the reasons of things that are from nothing.' The editor renders it 'the reasons of things that come from nothing having been surpassed'; Maximus often says 'of things that are', but 'from not-being' certainly where it is opposed absolutely to 'that which is'. Picus renders it badly: 'We suffer, when we have wholly gone beyond the discourses which are customarily held about things that are not', where there is not a grain of sense; and he gives a similarly mistaken rendering of Maximus's lofty teaching about deification in the homeland, 'becoming that which in no way exists as a right act of natural power'. The editor takes it thus: having attained that splendid deed of natural faculty which subsists nowhere, a fine deed indeed, which is nothing. Rather, what we undergo is that to which we are made, namely God, being made gods by deification, and this is by no means a deed or work of natural faculty (since it comes by that blessed passion) but of the most singular divine gift, God thus subjecting creation to himself, impressing his own image on it in creating it, and making it akin to himself by the faculty of understanding and free choice.

unplaced.en: On 'seeking out their reasons as types of intelligibles.' The editor glosses: he seeks out their reasons by the mind, as the forms of the intelligible. unplaced.en: On 'having the power of thinking and being thought, entirely at leisure.' The editor takes 'vacant, idle' (as already 'above thought') to mean that the mind has the power of the soul by which it thinks of itself or anything else, rather suffering a divine inflowing by which it is already made and becomes god. This is Maximus's plain meaning, expressed in countless places and most familiar to all mystics, as in the phrase 'having become above the being of things, to receive the illumination of the divine and unconquerable monad', as in ch. 95 of the preceding Century. Picus, in the opposite sense, 'strives with all his strength to understand and to be understood', which would be 'busy' (ascholazousan), and is quite alien; Picus's mind has not advanced far enough for the mystics' silence, leisure and darkness, and is busy with natural contemplation without rising spiritually to God. The editor adds that Maximus's explanation here and in ch. 11 of 'diakrithe' as 'were divided' departs from the common one: the Vulgate and Erasmus render 'kai me diakrithe' 'and shall not doubt', which the following 'but shall believe' (faith of miracles, opposed to hesitation and distrust) suggested, and Suidas glosses 'diakrinetai' as 'is in doubt, disbelieves'; but the first sense (divided) pleased Maximus more, since it was apter to ground a mystic sense, though there is a kind of division in unbelief and distrust too, whereby it becomes an obstacle to divine power, since the doubter does not cling firmly but is divided by thoughts.

unplaced.text: Ἡ τοῦ νοῦ δύναμις. Sic emend. ex mss. cod. cum esset, Ἡ τοῦ νόμου δύναμις. Hæc enim mentis objecta sunt, non legis : corporum incorporeorumque ( seu spirituum ) notitia : non tamen ipsius Trinitatis, quoad quod quid est esse, cognitio. Unum hoc credit pia mens, ipsam esse οὐ τί ποτε κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ἐστὶν αὐθαδιζομένη · sibi ipsa per superbiam non arrogans, ut sciat quid illa sit per essentiam ; ὡς ὁ δαιμόνιος νοῦς · quasi hoc uni proprium dicat divinæ menti. Nihil boni Picus : Nullatenus secundum substantiam est contumax, velut infelix animus. De voce δαιμόνιος, multa Bud. et alii. Planus hic sensus, ut sit divina ac beata mens, ipse Deus, qui sic a se nihil arrogatam habet sui per essentiam notitiam : quod tamen, et sequentia ejus cap. desiderant tres Regii codd. quorum copia fuit. Si quis tamen ad diabolum trahere velit, qui sic αὐθαδίζεσθαι dicatur, ut est illius a peccato ἄνους ὁ λόγος, et alia quæ prosequitur Dionys. non pugno. Potest ille temeritate adyta velle perrumpere et inconcessa tentare : at non sana mens, ac quæ nititur fide.
unplaced.anchorLine: μις (f) · τῆς δὲ τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος, κατὰ μόνην τὴν
unplaced.en: Hē tou nou dynamis ('the power of the mind'). So emended from a manuscript codex; when it read 'the power of the law' (nomou). For these are objects of the mind, not of the law: knowledge of bodies and of incorporeal things (that is, spirits), but not of the Trinity itself as to knowledge of what it is. This one thing the pious mind believes, that it is 'in no way self-willed according to essence', not arrogating to itself through pride to know what it is by essence, as the 'demonic mind' does, as though he were saying that this belongs to the divine mind alone. Picus is no good here: his 'in no way is it contumacious according to substance, like an unhappy soul'. On the word daimonios, Budé and others say much. The sense here is plain: that the divine and blessed mind, God himself, who thus claims for himself no knowledge of himself by essence that he has not; but three royal codices, of which there was a supply, lack this and the following of the chapter. If anyone nevertheless wished to apply it to the devil, who is said thus to be self-willed, as his reason (logos) is senseless from sin, and the other things Dionysius pursues, I do not object. He may with rashness want to break into the inner sanctuaries and attempt what is forbidden; but not a sound mind, one that rests on faith.

unplaced.text: Λάκκους καλεῖ ἡ Γραφή. Lacus ac cisternas expressit Scriptura, intellexitque Maximus ; nec bene Picus puteis mutavit. Puteus namque ipse fons est, sed alta scaturigine ; λάκκοι, lacus et cisternæ, non sunt fontes, nec ullo latice manant, sed pluvialibus aquis replentur. Qua metaphora φερομένης ἄνωθεν τῆς ἐν πνεύματι γνώσεως, scientia spiritali e supernis, e cœlo veniente, has mystice cisternas, Maximus ait impleri. At nihil bene Picus. Plena sunt spiritali sursum tendente scientia. Sursum tendere et salire, id quidem fontium est, vivarumque in eis aquarum, at non Maximo intentum, vel ejus Græcis significatum. Cf. ad Thalass. q. 48.
unplaced.anchorLine: νθʹ. Λάκκους καλεῖ ἡ Γραφὴ (i), τὰς δεκτικὰς τῶν
unplaced.en: Lakkous kalei hē Graphē ('Scripture calls them lakkoi'). Scripture expressed 'lakes and cisterns', and Maximus understood it so; Picus did not do well to change it to 'wells'. For a well is itself a spring, with deep welling; but lakkoi, 'pits and cisterns', are not springs, nor do they flow from any stream, but are filled with rainwater. By this metaphor, knowledge in the Spirit being borne from above (spiritual knowledge from on high, coming from heaven), Maximus says these cisterns are mystically filled. But Picus is wrong throughout: 'they are full of spiritual knowledge tending upward.' To tend upward and leap is characteristic of springs and of the living waters in them, but not what Maximus intended, nor what his Greek signifies. Compare the Ad Thalassium, question 48.

unplaced.en: Ta aisthēta panta ('all the sensibles'). Picus followed a disordered text and rendered nothing aptly: 'that is, all the sense-objects of the soul'. unplaced.text: Διὰ τῆς ἀοριστίας. Significat hujus scientiæ, quam ἄληστον vocat, quasi animo indelebilem semperque in eo vigentem ; immensam quamdam vim, qua animus divinam infinitatem quadam velut proportione attingat, ejusque veritatis gloriam ac majestatem omni majorem infinito, quasi simulacro referat. Nam et τὸ ἀόριστον, Maximo aliisque theologis, inter divina nomina est, id ipsum quod Latinis immensitas. Hæc tam augusta, quis ex Pico audiat : Ex illa incertitudine superinfinitam effingit opinionem veritatis ? Quid hic incertitudo, ubi Deus altissimo modo attingitur ? Num quod δόξα, eaque incertitudinem exposcit ? At non hæc philosophica δόξα, opinio ; nutans scilicet animi assensus, cui falsum potest subesse, nec raro subest ; sed ipsa animorum circa Deum ἀεικινησία ; in beatis jam consummata ; hic in summis θεωρητικοῖς, quasi incepta.
unplaced.anchorLine: εἰκονίζει διὰ τῆς ἀοριστίας (o) τὴν ὑπεράπει-
unplaced.en: Dia tēs aoristias ('through indefiniteness'). It signifies this knowledge, which he calls 'unforgettable' (alēston), as if indelible in the mind and always flourishing in it; a certain immense power by which the mind, through a kind of proportion, reaches the divine infinity and represents, as in an image, the glory and majesty of that truth, greater than every infinite. For to aoriston too, in Maximus and other theologians, is among the divine names, that which Latins call 'immensity'. Who could hear, from Picus, such lofty matter rendered as 'from that uncertainty it fashions a superinfinite opinion of the truth'? What uncertainty is here, where God is reached in the highest manner? Does doxa demand uncertainty? But this is not the philosophical doxa, 'opinion', that is, a wavering assent of the mind to which falsehood can be present, and often is; rather it is the minds' own ceaseless motion toward God (aeikinēsia), already perfected in the blessed, here begun in the highest contemplatives.

Clara allusio est ad I Esdr. iv, ubi describitur conatus hostium Judæorum, ut impedirent ædificationem templi ; quos Maximus tropologice dæmonas exponit, sic et ipsos et invidia contabescentes, quod spiritale in nobis Dei templum consurgere audiant, videantque, uti pluribus quæst. 56, ad Thal. Male itaque Picus διακονουμένους, dæmones habent hujusmodi voci inservientes. Non certe id muneris dæmonum ; etsi et ipsi simulate adjutores præferant exstruendi in nobis templi Domini, qui et hostes Judæorum, cum boni specie ac præstandæ virtutis, incautos spiritales in mali alicujus consensum trahunt, seu a recta virtutis via abducunt.

unplaced.en: Tē toiautē tēkomenous phōnē ('wasting away at such a voice'). A clear allusion to 1 Esdras 4 [sic as printed], where the attempt of the Jews' enemies to hinder the building of the temple is described; Maximus explains these tropologically as the demons, who likewise waste away with envy when they hear and see the spiritual temple of God rising in us, as is shown at greater length in question 56 of the Ad Thalassium. So Picus is wrong in rendering diakonoumenous: 'demons who have such a voice serving it'. It is certainly not the demons' office, even if they too pretend to be helpers in building the Lord's temple in us, who, like the enemies of the Jews, with an appearance of good and of virtue to be shown, draw the unwary spiritual into consent to some evil or lead them away from the right path of virtue. (The editor reports a reading in the printed text, 'tēkomenous', which differs from the printed Greek 'diatētēkomenous'; and rejects Picus's rendering.)

Sermonem sapientiæ, ut dignissimum primo loco ponit Apostolus I Cor. viii, λόγον σοφίας ; hincque Maximus μείζονα dicere, maluerit, quam μείζονος λόγον σοφίας : tanquam principem sapientiæ sermonem, non majoris sapientiæ sermonem. unplaced.anchorLine: βοῶν ἀλαλήτως (r)
unplaced.en: Boōn alalētōs ('crying out unutterably'). As if not with the tongue, or with a shout from the mouth, but one set in a greater contention of virtue and knowledge, as Maximus himself explains. So in Romans 8: 'stenagmois alalētois', Vulgate 'with unspeakable groanings'; it could also be 'silent in spirit'. Here the angel is the helper and saviour, whom Maximus calls 'a greater word of wisdom and knowledge' (meizona sophias kai gnōseōs logon). Picus: 'a word of wisdom and surpassing knowledge'. To me, more simply, 'the greater (that is, the chief) word of wisdom and knowledge'; as here, so too in chapter 20, in the phrase 'logos of knowledge' which is not at all 'greater' except by comparison to the rest that follow. For 'greater' does not mean a larger or more excellent word, speech or reason, wisdom and knowledge; but in them there is greater excellence and intensity. The Apostle in 1 Cor. 8 [as printed] puts 'the word of wisdom' in first place as most worthy; and hence Maximus would prefer to say meizona rather than meizonos logon sophias, meaning the chief word of wisdom, not the word of a greater wisdom. Also in chapter 41 he places supreme perfection in wisdom, which is itself the end and has an immediate relation to God.

Mens ergo laudabiliter moritur, cum sic se habet ad res alias, ac si ne esset quidem ; quod illis superatis, uni Deo et auctori tota impenditur. Non satis Picus, spontaneam omnium quæ sunt privationem ; quæ esset paupertatis definitio, non excellentiæ ejus status, quem Maximus intendit describere. Hesych. ἀπογενόμενοι, ἀποθανόντες.

unplaced.en: Tēn pros panta ta onta gnōmikēn apogenesin ('the gnomic departure-from-being with respect to all things'). As genesis is 'nature', and gignesthai is 'to arise, to be brought forth into the nature of things', so apogenesis is 'cessation and nothingness'. The mind thus dies laudably when it stands so toward other things as if they were not even there; which things being surpassed, the whole is spent on God alone and its author. Picus is not satisfactory with 'a spontaneous privation of all things that are'; that would be a definition of poverty, not of the excellence of the state which Maximus means to describe. Hesychius: 'apogenomenoi' = 'apothanontes' (those who have died).

Itaque ponit Maximus similitudinis rationem in imitatione divinæ bonitatis, quæ sit in nobis virtutum cultu et actione : imaginis vero rationem, in perfectissima illa omnium circa Deum uniformi scientia, quæ expressio sit divinæ veritatis. Non bene Picus : In quæ pro similitudine relucere solet quoddam ornamentum : quasi τὸ, ἐν ᾗ, referat τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς, non τὸ, συμπλήρωσις τῆς θείας ἐνεργείας. Utrumque sane et similitudo et imago, in anima elucet, non pro ejus substantia (quod attinet ad Maximi hic scopum) sed prout vel virtute vel scientia pollet, Deique in se bonitatem ac veritatem utraque refert.
unplaced.anchorLine: πέφυκε κάλλος (z) ·
unplaced.en: En hē to kath' homoiōsin anaphainesthai pephyke kallos ('in which the beauty according to likeness is by nature made to appear'). In this completion of the divine operation the beauty of likeness shines forth, which is to say what belongs to likeness. Maximus thus places the principle of likeness in the imitation of divine goodness, which is in us through the cultivation and practice of the virtues; and the principle of image in that most perfect, uniform knowledge of all things concerning God, which is the expression of divine truth. Picus is wrong: 'in the things for which a certain ornament is wont to shine as likeness', as if 'in which' (en hē) referred to what belongs to the soul, and not to 'the completion of the divine operation'. Both likeness and image shine in the soul, not according to its substance (which is not Maximus's concern here) but as it is strong in virtue or knowledge, and each represents God's goodness and truth in it.

Verum hæc ex Hebr. non prodierunt immediate. Hebr. unum idemque nomen est, quod statim seq. timor redditur. Ac forte scripserint οἱ LXX πνεῦμα εὐλαβείας : qui sit spiritus timoris casti, modesti, reverentialis ac religiosi. Videtur hic Maximus ἐπιστήμην pro prudentia usurpare, ac particulari judicio agibilium ; ut et γνῶσιν, pro judicio universali, ac quo rerum rationes comprehendamus. Alioqui notum quid ἐπιστήμη, et scientia stricte dictæ, philosophis.
unplaced.anchorLine: πνεῦμα γνώσεως, πνεῦμα ἐπιστήμης (b), πνεῦμα
unplaced.en: Pneuma epistēmēs ('spirit of knowledge'). The Septuagint has 'spirit of piety' (eusebeias); the Vulgate 'spirit of piety'. Maximus himself, in century 4, in these five at chapters 79 and 80, also has 'spirit of piety'. The Arabic: 'of true religion'. But these did not come immediately from the Hebrew. In the Hebrew it is one and the same word, which is immediately afterward rendered 'fear'. And perhaps the Seventy wrote 'spirit of reverence' (eulabeias): which is the spirit of chaste, modest, reverential and religious fear. Maximus here seems to use epistēmē for prudence, and for particular judgement of matters to be done; as also gnōsis for universal judgement, by which we comprehend the principles of things. Otherwise it is well known what epistēmē is, and what knowledge in the strict sense is, for philosophers. (The editor offers a conjecture on the Septuagint reading: eulabeias for eusebeias.)

unplaced.text: Πρὸς τὸ τῆς σοφίας τέλος τὴν σύνεσιν. Singularis hic videtur vocis τέλος acceptio. Non enim intelligentia et σύνεσις proprie finis est sapientiæ, cum hæc perfectior sit omniumque absolutio, qua ipsi immediate unimur Deo; sed ultimum est et quasi limes, ὅρος, quo postremo sapientiam nanciscimur, nec aliud Maximus hac loquendi forma voluerit ; ultimum scilicet ad eam gradus. Qui velit τέλος hic, effectum, esse, quam ejus vocis significationem inter primas illius ponit Thesaurus, nec is a vero abierit. Sic enim, c. 44, sapientiam monada seu unitatem exponit Maximus, ex qua virtutes reliquæ intelligantur procedere, in quibus origine prima ἡ σύνεσις, ipsa quo ad nos ultima, qua incipientes a timore gradum ad sapientiam facimus, quæ est illa virtutum ad ipsam ἀποκατάστασις, seu revocatio : quod utrumque Maximus, ut subtilissimus, in mente habuerit.
unplaced.anchorLine: πρὸς τὸ τῆς σοφίας τέλος τὴν σύνεσιν (c), ἀναβαίνο-
unplaced.en: Pros to tēs sophias telos tēn synesin ('toward the end of wisdom, understanding'). A singular use of the word telos seems to occur here. For intelligence and synesis is not properly the end of wisdom, since wisdom is the more perfect and the completion of all things, by which we are immediately united to God; rather it is the last and, as it were, the boundary (horos), at which finally we attain wisdom; and Maximus would have meant nothing else by this manner of speaking: the last step toward it. If anyone wishes telos here to mean 'effect', which the Thesaurus puts among the first meanings of the word, he would not go astray. For thus in chapter 44 Maximus explains wisdom as a monad, that is, a unity, from which the other virtues are understood to proceed, among which synesis is first in origin and, as to us, last, by which, beginning from fear, we take a step toward wisdom, which is the restoration (apokatastasis) or recall of the virtues to it: both of which Maximus, being most subtle, would have had in mind.

Picus is not good: 'The boy and the girl are doing business', whereas they rather undertake, or have, and as I rendered it, 'they labour'. 'The sixth of the years': 'the sixfold number of years'. The earlier editions had 'aretōn' (of the virtues), 'virtutum', though Picus worked it out. For what are the six virtues? Philosophers know four, theologians three; neither six: nor is this number consecrated in virtues; it is itself in other respects perfect, and a symbol of action because the world was made in six days, with the seventh devoted to rest, which is the day of the Sabbath; a new creation for us begun on the Lord's day by his resurrection and our own in it, in the verse: 'on whose eve (prosortion), on the great Sabbath, I wrote these notes while rereading, on the Kalends of April, indiction 16.' unplaced.en: "Ἡ ἄρρητος περιχώρησις τοῦ πεπιστευμένου" (the ineffable interpenetration of what is believed). The word has another sense in profane usage than the one that fits here. Picus's rendering, 'arcana processio' (hidden procession), does not satisfy, and I do not quite see what he means by the word. Budaeus, far more learned, in the Damascene on the Trinity renders the divine persons' perichoresis as 'union', which is perhaps a little loose; theologians call it circumincession, as if one person's passing into another on every side; I would prefer 'that one takes in the other and as it were contains and comprehends it', as the divine persons are also said to proceed inseparably (anekphoitos), so that one does not go outside the other: the verb chorein has a very common meaning and is also used of the mind, which understands by containing and holding the thing in itself. So I understand Maximus thus: the manifestation and revelation of the thing believed and of God (which comes about through the gifts of the Spirit that aid faith) is our comprehension and perception of him, so that we have him dwelling in us and know him present and most intimate to us, according to Paul (Eph. iii, 17): 'that Christ dwell by faith in your hearts.' Nor does this forbid calling it a hidden union and as it were a commingling, as Hesychius explains perichorei as 'is mingled'. But in these matters we stammer, though the Greeks are somewhat better off than we in vocabulary. Elsewhere Picus is hardly happier, as when he renders 'aeikinetos stasis' as 'a condition ever moving', and not as a stability driven by perpetual motion, such as that of those who enjoy God.

unplaced.text: Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν. Nulla hic commodius voce reddi videatur, quam si intentionalem dicamus; quasi in animi rationibus et apprehensione positam; quam et abstractivam rudiori vocabulo nostri theologi vocant. Affinis usus illius vocis Patribus vii synodi, dum adorationem imaginum, quam sanciunt, σχετικήν vocant; quæ scilicet non ad ipsam rem, ut in se est, terminatur, sed ut in sui similitudine, animo cogitanti quasi præsens objicitur, ac quadam in eam intentione ac motu, secundum quam dicitur honor imaginis transire ad exemp'ar seu prototypum. Nihil ad rem, quod Picus semel et iterum reconditam. Ac certe longe inauditum mundo, quod quis ex ejus interpretamentis conficeret vocabularium: sic sine judicio cuncta viro arbitraria; ut quod hic, ἡ μεθέξει κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις, illi cognitio est particeps operationis: quod ἔφεσιν, pro αἴσθησιν decoquit, etc.
unplaced.anchorLine: τὴν μέν, σχετικὴν (o), ὡς ἐν λόγῳ μόνῳ κειμένην
unplaced.en: "Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν" (the relational one). No word seems to render it better here than 'intentional', as if lodged in the soul's reckonings and apprehension; our theologians also call it, in a cruder term, 'abstractive'. The Fathers of the seventh council use the word in a kindred way when they call the veneration of images that they sanction 'relational': it does not terminate in the thing itself as it is in itself, but is set before the thinking mind as if present in its likeness, with a certain intention and movement toward it, according to which the honor of the image is said to pass to the exemplar or prototype. Picus's 'reconditam' (hidden), repeated again and again, is beside the point. And it is certainly unheard of anywhere that someone should compile a vocabulary from his renderings: so everything becomes arbitrary to the man without judgment; as here, where the Greek 'ἡ μεθέξει κατ᾽ ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις' becomes in him 'knowledge that is a partaker of operation', and 'ἔφεσιν' he boils down to 'αἴσθησιν', and so on.

unplaced.text: Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως. Quod semel et iterum cavet Maximus, hoc et 39 cap. ne τὸ ἀναιτίως et ἀναίτιον, quasi innoxium et sine culpa accipiatur, quæ est proclivis ejus vocis acceptio, id vero propense Picus amplectitur, ac ubique interpretatur. Est certe hæc voluptas eo sensu haud ἀναίτιος, sed culpæ conjuncta, et ex culpa, ni magis ipsa culpa; ipse naturæ reatus ex transgressione, sic quasi brutæ vitæ, quæ libidine ducatur, nec jam ratione, sed magis sensu vivat: ἀναίτιος vero, id est sine causa, quod laborem, cui succedat, ejusque causa sit, nullum habeat. Unde nec Christus sic ἀναίτιον nativitatem ex libidine assumpsit, quod non illo modo ἀναίτιος, sed illi comitem laborem, exque illa, ὡς αἰτίας, ut eo juste, cum in illo injustus esset, nullo scilicet in ipso reatu, illam aboleret. Quam belle cohæret, ut Maximo ἀδικωτάτῃ, injustissima, sit hæc voluptas seu libido, et tamen ipsa ἀναίτιος sit, ipsa sine culpa, bello interprete Pico? Nec enim ut labor injustus, sic et voluptas; quod hæc a voluntate exsistat, ille ab exteriore agente.
unplaced.anchorLine: προκαθηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως (p). Ἀναίτιον δέ φημι
unplaced.en: "Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως" (it went before birth without cause). Maximus guards, here and again in ch. 39, against taking anaitios and anaition as 'harmless' and 'without fault', which is the easy sense of the word, and which Picus eagerly adopts and renders everywhere. This pleasure is certainly not 'blameless' in that sense, but is joined to fault and arises from fault, if not itself the fault; it is nature's own liability from the transgression, as of a brute life led by lust and no longer by reason but rather by sense. 'Anaitios' properly means 'without cause', in that it has no labor following it and caused by it. So Christ did not take a birth from lust in that sense of 'anaition', but rather took labor as its companion, and by it, as by a cause, justly abolished the pleasure, since he was unjust in no way, having no liability in himself. How well it holds together, then, that for Maximus this pleasure or lust is 'most unjust' (adikotate), and yet is itself 'anaitios', itself without fault, as Picus handsomely translates! For pleasure is not unjust as labor is; this arises from the will, that from an external agent.

Quod sic hic, et sequenti cap. ac passim alibi Maximus naturam ingerit, ejusque rationem ut virtutis omnis regulam, ac necessitudinis cum Deo normam; ut tantum Deo uniamur ac virtute fulgeamus, simusque capaces æternæ beatitudinis, quantum nobis ac nostræ voluntati cum naturæ rationibus convenerit; de natura sanata et instituta per gratiam, omnino intelligendum non de ipsa quatenus in nobis ex transgressione pro peccato inolevit: de natura demum qualis a Deo condita fuit, imagine ornata et similitudine, in qua divini elucerent characteres, non cui obducta ex peccato brutorum ipsa πάθη (libidines scilicet), virtutis cultu ac exercitatione a nobis excutienda, ut divina in nobis instauretur vita, quod non aliter habemus, quam Christi gratia.

unplaced.en: "Οἱ μὲν τῇ φύσει." That Maximus thus brings in nature here and in the next chapter, and often elsewhere, and its principle as the rule of all virtue and the norm of our relation with God, so that we are united to God and shine with virtue, and are capable of eternal blessedness, just so far as our own wil[l ...] (the note breaks off at the foot of the page and continues on p-0678). [...as far as] our will agrees with the principles of nature. Where nature healed and restored through grace is meant, it must be understood not of nature as it has grown up in us through the transgression as a result of sin, but of nature as it was created by God, adorned with the image and likeness in which divine characters shone; not of nature overlaid by sin with the brutish passions (that is, lusts), which must be shaken off by us through the practice and exercise of virtue, so that the divine life be restored in us, which we have in no other way than by the grace of Christ.

Ipsa angelorum operatio, qua inferiores illuminant ac perficiunt, Dionysio θεουργία, ac si dicas, divinis dotibus imbuens. unplaced.en: 'Of true theurgy.' He seems here to mean true theurgy, or divine operation, which is thus completed by action and contemplation and as it were has the force of both eminently: that is, wisdom, which is nearest to deification. As to how, with Dionysius, theurgy is also said of Christ: nothing seems to prevent it, not indeed as understood to precede the union and dispose toward it (which is of Nestorian chaff), but as its companion and following upon it, like its adornment, in which same [theurgy] Christ is for us both author and most perfect exemplar; with his theurgy, as Budé explains, (Continuing from the previous page: '...as Budé explains,') '...[a theurgy] for the divine power and operation of miracles granted to few, and one that was not lacking to the Old Testament; but the theurgy by which we are raised to deification, the capacity for which is given to all reborn through Christ. Non enim circa γένεσιν absolute, sic libidinosa versatur mentis affectio, sed circa γένεσιν ἐπείσακτον, quæ ex peccato advenit naturæ, et quam Maximus non raro γέννησιν vocat, opponitque τῇ γενέσει · quæ sit simplex procreatio et ortus, qualis a Deo Adami fuit, non qui brutorum more commistione seminum ac libidine in nobis fit; quod passim Maximus post Greg Nyss. ac superiores theologos negat futurum homine non peccante. As for the word γνωμικῶς (by which Maximus teaches how the spiritual circumcision truly acceptable to God is to be performed), [Picus] rendered it cleverly; Picus, not clever enough, rendered it 'est animo, voluntate'; and what I have rendered is 'by the mind's choice and the soul's judgment.' Allegoria est, ejus quod psal. illo lxiv habetur, Εὐλογήσεις τὸν στέφανον τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τῆς χρηστότητός σου, ubi χρηστότης ex parte Dei se tenet ejusque benignitatem ac clementiam sonat, qua sic annum bonis instruit, ut sit amicis quasi contexta corona : ita hic fides, tantis aucta muneribus, quanta describit Maximus. Nec satis aptum videtur quod reddit Picus, corona probitatis, quod sic nemo in eo psal. interpretatus est, ac merito ; nec enim dici potest, corona probitatis Dei, sed ejus benignitatis seu bonitatis ; non qua coronetur Dei probitas, sed qua Deus benignitate coronat ac bonitate.
unplaced.anchorLine: μδ'. Στέφανός ἐστι χρηστότητος (g), πίστις κα-
unplaced.en: 'Crown of kindness.' This is an allusion to what is found in Psalm lxiv: 'You will bless the crown of the year of your kindness (χρηστότης)'; there χρηστότης belongs on God's side and denotes his benignity and clemency, by which he so furnishes the year with good things that it is as it were a woven crown for his friends; so here faith is enlarged with gifts as great as Maximus describes. What Picus renders, 'crown of probity,' seems not quite apt, since no one has so interpreted that psalm, and rightly: for one cannot say 'crown of God's probity,' but [crown] of his benignity or goodness; not that God's probity is crowned, but that God crowns with benignity and goodness. No bracketed word is at issue.

unplaced.text: Ἣν οἶδεν ὁ λόγος. Quod sic vocat Maximus, ὁ λόγος, non ipsa sacra Scriptura est, sed Dionysius, qui sic de angelis loquitur; ut quasi fundatam eorum circa Deum collocationem ac sedem significet, quæ erit et hominum beatorum, quibus Deus ipse locus futurus sit ; ex quo etiam, perennis illa ejusdem motus quies et stabilitas ; cum in tempore, quo agimus, ipso alterante, jugis sit mutatio.
unplaced.anchorLine: λόγος (h) ἄμεσον εἶναι περὶ τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον, τῶν
unplaced.en: 'Which the Word knows.' What Maximus here calls 'the Word' (ὁ λόγος) is not Holy Scripture itself but Dionysius, who speaks so of the angels, as if to signify their established placing and seat about God, which will also be that of the blessed among men, to whom God himself will be the place; whence also the perennial rest and stability of that same motion, whereas in time, in which we act, time itself changing, there is constant alteration. No bracketed word is at issue.

unplaced.text: Τὴν κατὰ πρόθεσιν κίνησιν. Etiam quæst. illa 65, cum perspicuum sit leg. κένωσιν, seu magis χύσιν · nec Maximum aliter scripsisse. De vitæ enim carnalis sacrificio sanguinis metaphora sermo est, quem liquet non aliter quam libatione et fusione offerri. Nihil ergo ad rem, quod ita Picus reddidit, velut commotionem sanguinis, etc. Sane cohærent νέκρωσις et κένωσις, alterum in viventibus, alterum quasi in humidis et fluentibus ; κίνησις, ne vel minimum.
unplaced.anchorLine: πρόθεσιν κίνησιν (i), ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν
unplaced.en: 'The motion according to purpose.' Question 65 likewise, since it is clear that one should read κένωσις ('emptying') or rather χύσις ('pouring out'); and Maximus did not write otherwise. For the discourse is a metaphor of the sacrifice of the life of the flesh by blood, which, as is clear, is offered only by libation and pouring. So Picus's rendering 'as it were the commotion of blood' etc., is beside the point. Indeed νέκρωσις ('mortification') and κένωσις cohere, the one among living things, the other as among liquids and fluids; κίνησις ('motion') not in the least. (The editor gives a VARIANT/CONJECTURE: read κένωσιν or χύσιν for κίνησιν; the printed text has κίνησιν unbracketed.)

unplaced.text: Πρὸς τὴν θείαν λῆξιν ὁλοκαυτουμένων. Ut Deo totæ cedant : hæc enim holocausti ratio, ut omnia Deo adoleantur, nullæque vel sacerdotis vel offerentium partes fiant ; cujusmodi Maximus nostrum hic describit sacrificium. Est enim λῆξις, μερίς, uti Suidas exponit, et quod quis sortitur eique obtingit ac illius juris exsistit. Non bene itaque Picus, ad divinam sortem consequendum : non enim adjunctum, eum sensum patitur ; etsi alias illa vox ipsum admittat ; sitque vere Deus ipse nostra λῆξις, τὸ, παῦσις, id est, hæreditas, κληρονομία, ipso Suida interprete ; dicimusque sanctos μακαρίαν λῆξιν, beatas sedes adeptos esse. Nec bene Portus illud Suid. λῆξις, παῦσις, cessatio, sedatio, exponit : melius requies, quæ ipsa æterna, nostra in Deo hæreditas est.
unplaced.anchorLine: μένων (j).
unplaced.en: 'Towards the divine portion of those offered as holocausts.' So that they wholly yield to God: for this is the rationale of the holocaust, that everything be burnt for God and no parts fall to priest or offerers; such is the sacrifice Maximus describes here as ours. For λῆξις is 'share' (μερίς), as Suidas explains, and what one obtains by lot and falls to him and becomes his right. So Picus, 'to attain the divine lot,' is not good, since the adjoining context does not bear that sense, though the word elsewhere admits it; and God himself truly is our λῆξις, i.e. 'inheritance' (κληρονομία), by Suidas's own interpretation; and we say that the saints have obtained a 'blessed portion', blessed abodes. Nor does Portus do well with that word of Suidas, λῆξις, 'cessation, calming': better 'rest', which is itself eternal, our inheritance in God. No bracketed word is at issue.

unplaced.text: Ἐπιληπτευόμενον τοῖς ὑλικοῖς. Qui velut dæmone, sic terrenis eorumque amore teneatur, arreptitiorum more; dum hoc animus ipse patitur, quod Saul. corpore a dæmone, a quo mitius habebat, Davide pulsante citharam. Non bene Picus, Rebus materialibus, quasi morbo comitiali laboranti, quæ est altera hujus vocis acceptio, secundo loco Hesychio posita, καὶ ὁ τῇ ἱερᾷ νόσῳ συνεχόμενος · Qui sacro morbo, id est, comitiali, laborat. Sic enim laboranti non prodest mystici Davidis cithara, uti nec Sauli profuisset, si hic ejus fuisset morbus, cum auctore Traliano et experientia teste, sic correpti, nec audiant, nec videant, nec intelligant, sed omnium sensuum facultate destituti jaceant, nihil differentes a mortuis. At nec sequentia bene reddita, τὸ πονηρὸν πνεῦμα τῆς ὑλικῆς περιπετείας, Malignum spiritum temeritatis materialis. Τῆς πρὸς αἴσθησιν additum ex mss. terrenorum vicissitudo est eorumque συμπτώματα et casus, unde sic varie sensus afficitur, ac vitia nobis propignuntur : sic enim nobis hæc allegoria, πονηρὸν πνεῦμα, non materialium temeritas, quæ non tam materialium dicatur, quam intelligentium; nempe προπέτεια.
unplaced.anchorLine: γνώσεως, ἐπιληπτευόμενον τοῖς ὑλικοῖς (k) τὸν ἡμέ-
unplaced.en: 'Seized by epilepsy among material things.' Seized as if by a demon, so held by earthly things and by love of them, in the manner of the possessed, while the soul itself suffers this, as Saul did in body from the demon, whom he bore more mildly when David played the harp. Picus does not render well, 'Rebus materialibus, quasi morbo comitiali laboranti' ('by material things, as one suffering from the falling sickness'), which is the other meaning of the word, given second place by Hesychius, 'one held by the sacred disease,' i.e. one who suffers epilepsy. For David's mystical harp does not help one so afflicted, as it would not have helped Saul had this been his disease, as Trallian [Alexander] attests and experience bears out: those so seized neither hear nor see nor understand but lie deprived of all sensory faculty, no different from the dead. Nor are the following words well rendered: 'the evil spirit of material misfortune' (τὸ πονηρὸν πνεῦμα τῆς ὑλικῆς περιπετείας) [Picus has] 'the evil spirit of material rashness.' The words 'τῆς πρὸς αἴσθησιν' ('that toward sense-perception') the editor SUPPLIES, added from manuscripts: [the phrase means] the vicissitude of earthly things and their accidents and chances, whence the sense is variously affected and vices are engendered in us; for so for us this allegory is 'the evil spirit', not 'the rashness of material things', which is said not so much of material things as of intelligent beings, namely προπέτεια ('rashness'). (The supplied words stand unbracketed in the text.)

unplaced.text: Οὐδεμία ἐμφέρεια τούτων πρὸς ἄλληλα. Picus, ut sunt illi omnia arbitraria : Nulla horum cognatio est. Effectuum scilicet et causarum. At certe novere poetæ, quorum Paulus Act. xvii, dictum refert, probatque, Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν : Ipsius et genus sumus ; ab ipso scilicet ducta cognatione, qua et Patrem vitæque auctorem ipsum habemus, imagine etiam insigniti et similitudine ; qua divinæ ipsæ dotes in nobis elucent, libertas arbitrii, et quæ huic virtutes comites sunt, præexsistuntque in Deo περισσῶς καὶ οὐσιωδῶς, ut seq. cap. Maximus ; abundanter (seu excellenter et eximie) et essentialiter ; in nobis vero, deficienter et participatione : ex quo est, ut nulla sit inter nos Deumque ἐμφέρεια : exacta scilicet similitudo, ac qualem vox illa importat ; ut sic unum alterum referat, ut quasi pro eo accipi possit ; quo spectant illa Domini verba Joan. xiv : Ὁ ἐμὲ ἑωρακὼς, ἑώρακε καὶ τὸν Πατέρα : Qui vidit me, vidit et Patrem ; cujus ἐκμαγεῖον perfectaque expressio erat, naturalis Patris naturalis Filius. Ne cui vero durior sermo videretur, quasi ἐμφέρεια sit quovis modo dicta ὁμοιότης, similitudo, quæ non omnino neganda videtur inter causas et effecta, seq. cap. velut molliens, Οὐκ ἔστιν, inquit, ἀκριβὴς ἐμφέρεια : Non est exacta repræsentatio et similitudo : ubi Pic. perinde malus interpres : Non est explorata connexio. Nugæ : ut et quod τὰς ἐνδεχομένας εἰκόνας reddit, occurrentes imagines ; pro quantas licet, vel quantas creatura referre possit ; quantæ sunt possibiles. His se fæcibus ac stercoribus impleant, quibus Græca nec aspicere libet, ut ipsam vere Patrum mentem intelligant.
unplaced.anchorLine: οὐδεμία δὲ ἐμφέρεια τούτων πρὸς ἄλληλα (l), αἰτίων
unplaced.en: 'No likeness (ἐμφέρεια) of these to one another.' Picus, as is his way, makes everything arbitrary: 'There is no kinship between them' -- of effects, that is, and causes. But surely the poets knew it, whose saying Paul reports and approves, Acts xvii: 'For we are also his offspring' -- kinship drawn from him, through which we have him as Father and author of life, and are marked with his image and likeness, through which the divine gifts themselves shine in us, freedom of choice and the virtues that accompany it, which pre-exist in God 'abundantly and essentially' (as Maximus says in the next chapter), 'in an eminent and exceptional way', whereas in us they exist deficiently and by participation; hence no ἐμφέρεια, that is, exact likeness of the kind that word implies, so that one would reproduce the other and could be taken for it, exists between us and God. To this look the Lord's words in John xiv, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' [the Son being the exact impression and perfect expression of the Father, the natural Son of a natural Father]. Lest the language seem too harsh, as if ἐμφέρεια were in any way called ὁμοιότης ('likeness'), which seems not wholly deniable between causes and effects, Maximus in the next chapter, softening it, says 'There is no exact ἐμφέρεια': 'no exact representation and likeness'; here Picus is equally a bad interpreter with 'There is no explored connection.' Nonsense; so too his rendering of τὰς ἐνδεχομένας εἰκόνας as 'occurring images', for 'as many as is permitted' or 'as many as the creature can bear'; 'as many as are possible.' Let them fill themselves with these dregs and dung (at which one does not care to look in Greek), that they may truly understand the mind of the Fathers. (No bracketed word is at issue.)

unplaced.text: Τὸν παρόντα τῶν σκαμμάτων αἰῶνα. Quod in Pico exstat, præsens scenæ sæculum, typographicum mendum puto, ac eum arenæ scripsisse, quam et ego vocem, Græcæ vocis explicandæ causa adjeci. Utraque enim idem utrisque significatur locus certaminis ac fossa, in qua non esset ejus defugere aleam, sed vel cum adversario pugile decertandum, vel cum bestiis depugnandum, in quibus tale certamen gentilium feritate exhibebatur ; quod nihil cum scena, ut liquet, habet commune. Quod vero sequitur, ὅλοι ὅλῳ Θεῷ ἐγκραθῆναι, toti in toto Deo firmari, id vero ipsius Pici inscitiæ, dum non advertit τὸ, κραθεὶς et ἐγκραθεὶς, ἀπὸ τοῦ κεράννυμι esse, miscere, qua voce intima illa mentis cum Deo unio passim theologis significatur.
unplaced.anchorLine: παρόντα τῶν σκαμμάτων αἰῶνα (m) διέβησαν· τὴν
unplaced.en: 'The present age of the σκάμματα' (the wrestling-pits). What stands in Picus, 'the present age of the stage', I take to be a printer's error, and that he wrote 'of the arena' (arenæ), a word I too added to explain the Greek word. For both words signify the same thing, the place of contest, the pit in which one could not shirk the hazard, but must fight either with an adversary as boxer or struggle with wild beasts, in which such combat was displayed with the savagery of the heathen; which, as is clear, has nothing in common with the stage. As to what follows, 'ὅλοι ὅλῳ Θεῷ ἐγκραθῆναι', which Picus renders 'to be made firm, all in the whole God', that is Picus's own ignorance, since he does not notice that κραθείς and ἐγκραθείς come from κεράννυμι, 'to mix', the word by which the mind's inmost union with God is everywhere signified by theologians.

unplaced.text: Ἐνέργειαν δὲ, τὸ νόημα. Varia ejus vocis acceptio, sæpius Maximo discussa ; ea occasione, quod pro ipsa operatione vel facultate, una in Christo asserebatur, his qui proxime Eutychiano errori accedebant, qua ἀνενέργητον humanam in Christo naturam ponebant, ipsam tollentes, siquidem nihil in natura est, non naturali præditum facultate. Hic ἐνέργειαν, ipsum dicit intellectionis terminum ac verbum, in quo mens rem intueretur. Anastasiam exponit Maximus, dum unam ipse videtur velle ἐνέργειαν, pro effectu, in his quæ ex Vaticanis codd. ejus argumenti damus.

unplaced.anchorLine: ἐνέργειαν δὲ, τὸ νόημα (n). Πέρας γὰρ τοῦτο,
unplaced.en: 'And operation (energeia) is the thought.' The varied acceptation of this word, often discussed by Maximus; on the occasion that 'one operation' or faculty was asserted in Christ by those who came closest to the Eutychian error, who posited a human nature in Christ that was 'without operation' (ἀνενέργητον), thereby removing it, since nothing in nature exists that is not endowed with a natural faculty. Here he calls the 'energeia' itself the term and word of intellection, in which the mind looks at a thing. Maximus explains Anastasius (his 'one energeia') as meaning 'by effect', in the passages from the Vatican codices that we give on that subject.

unplaced.en: 'Unforthcoming from himself' (ἀνεκφοίτητος ἑαυτοῦ). Read thus entirely, in place of what stood (ἀνεκφοίτητον): a word Picus wrongly renders actively and refers to power, 'and never deserting', whereas it refers to God himself. Nothing is more usual in theology than that the divine processions are to be understood as 'not going forth' (ἀνεκφοιτήτως): so that through them the persons (or the Trinity itself in the processions outward) do not leave themselves by producing, even though they truly exist in what is produced, whether persons or things; yet otherwise persons in persons, otherwise the Trinity in things, of which Maximus here speaks: 'the abundant love of the good toward beings' (Picus ineptly: 'the highest love of good toward creatures'). The first reason why God is a jealous one is that he is endowed with the greatest force of good love toward things: for jealousy (zelus) is excess of love. Maximus has [all] learning on these [matters] [the note continues in the right column].

unplaced.anchorLine: ἁπλῆ καὶ ἀκίνητος (p)**οὖσα, καὶ
unplaced.en: 'Simple and unmoved.' I read what is found in the scholia to Dionysius and in Dionysius himself: αὐτοκίνητος ('self-moved'), for what is explained is the divine motion of love in himself and toward himself, whose likeness is our ever-moving (ἀεικίνητος) yearning toward him, a constant motion of desire. This Maximus says grandly: 'the erotic motion of the good, pre-existing in the good': the motion of love toward the good, itself prior and existing in the good; in God, that is, as in the exemplar, who is himself the good loving, and so loving the good, from which is every origin of love of the good. Picus is inelegant: 'the motion which is in the first place loving the good', etc. (The editor would read αὐτοκίνητος in place of the printed ἀκίνητος.)

Immobilis firmitas et sedes fundati in honesto situs sui, quod maxime justitiæ convenit ; quæ velut terra in hoc universo, suis undique librata momentis, rei ipsum medium immobiliter attendat, ac cuique, quod reipsa illius est, tribuat. unplaced.en: 'An unremovable seat according to the position of its base.' Immovable firmness and the seat of what is founded in the honourable placing of itself, which fits justice above all; which, like earth in this universe, poised on all sides by its own moments, attends to the very middle of the thing unmovably, and gives to each what truly is his. Picus nonetheless gets out of it: 'He places the seat of his own foundation, transferred, in the honourable'; if indeed this is getting out of it, to render so arbitrarily.

unplaced.text: Υἱὸν ἀποδειχθῆναι Θεοῦ. Quod deerat vox υἱόν, nihil commodum reddere potuit Picus : ἀπροαίρετον γένεσιν καὶ ὑλικήν, ortum nativitatis non ex libera voluntate et terrenum, quo naturaliter propagamur, ubique Maximus post Greg. Nyss. aliosque Græcos theologos, ex primi parentis transgressione nobis inolevisse docet : alio multiplicandi humani generis modo spiritaliori Deo non ignoto, integra etiam parentum virginitate ; quem August. fatetur se ignorare. Τὸ, ἀπροαίρετον, quod invitam reddit Picus, non satis aptum : sonat enim illa vox contrariam voluntatem et repugnantem, cum vox Græca solum liberæ voluntatis dicat absentiam, oppositione ad spiritalem generationem κατὰ προαίρεσιν ἐν πνεύματι : quæ ex libera voluntate est in spiritu, qua scilicet nascimur a Deo, ut ejus filii simus ac dii Deo similes.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἀποδειχθῆναι Θεοῦ (r) καὶ Θεὸν κατὰ τὴν χάριν θέσιν,
unplaced.en: 'To be shown a son of God.' Since the word υἱόν ('son') was missing [in the text], Picus could not render it suitably: 'a not-chosen and material genesis', the origin of a birth not from free will and earthly, by which we are naturally propagated; Maximus everywhere, after Gregory of Nyssa and other Greek theologians, teaches that it grew upon us from the transgression of the first parent, there being another, more spiritual, manner of multiplying the human race, not unknown to God, with the parents' virginity intact; which Augustine confesses he does not know. As for ἀπροαίρετον, which Picus renders 'unwilling' ('invitam'), it is not apt enough: that word sounds like a contrary and resisting will, whereas the Greek word says only the absence of free will, in opposition to the spiritual generation 'by choice in the Spirit': that which is from free will in the Spirit, by which we are born of God, so as to be his sons and gods like God. (The note supplies υἱόν, the missing word, in the text.)

unplaced.anchorLine: κῶν λόγων ὑποδεκτικὴ [edit. ἀποδεκτικὴ], τὴν ἐν
unplaced.en: VARIANT: the earlier edition read ἀποδεκτική ('acceptive') where the editor prints ὑποδεκτική ('receptive'). Neither a supply nor a deletion; the bracket reports the earlier reading.

unplaced.anchorLine: κατὰ τὴν θέσιν βάσεως ἀμετάθετος [male edita, μετάθετος] ἵδρυσις (q).
unplaced.en: PRIVATIVE BRACKET, p-0708: the printed text has ἀμετάθετος ('unremovable'); the bracket says the earlier edition, badly edited, had μετάθετος ('removable'), without the alpha privative. So the bracket gives a VARIANT that LACKS the privative; the editor's own text keeps ἀ-. It is not a supply and not a deletion by the editor: the editor corrects μετάθετος to ἀμετάθετος, and note (q) confirms ('Quod erat μετάθετος, valde mendosum est').

unplaced.text: Ἐκ περιστάσεως. Cap. sequenti περιστατικὴν ἀνάγκην vocat Maximus necessitatem ex ipsis vitæ mortalis rationibus, ejusque variis casibus ; quam levare artis præceptis studet humana solertia : hæc nempe indigentia, quam idem excludit a primi status felicitate, Καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς ὑπάρχων τῆς περὶ τέχνας περιστατικῆς ἐλεύθερος ἦν. Ubi male Picus, Καὶ προσδεὴς ὑπάρχων· Et cum egeret : quæ ratio est non absolvens ab artium cura, sed potius ei addicens. Alia pridem in aliis non bonis Maximi interpretibus mihi sugillata, unius litteræ seu syllabæ elisione, proclivi lapsu festinantis manus scribæ, decoquentibus quod palam Scripturæ adversetur, ac cujus contrarium Maximo serio adnotetur.
unplaced.anchorLine: λόγους τεχνῶν ἐκ περιστάσεως (s) διὰ τὴν χρείαν·
unplaced.en: 'From circumstance.' In the following chapter Maximus calls 'circumstantial necessity' (περιστατικὴν ἀνάγκην) the necessity arising from the very conditions of mortal life and its various chances, which human skill strives to relieve by the precepts of art: namely that indigence which he excludes from the happiness of the first state, 'And being without need (ἀπροσδεής), he was free of the circumstantial need concerning the arts.' Where Picus is wrong with 'Καὶ προσδεὴς ὑπάρχων', 'And when he was in need', a reading that does not release from the care of the arts but rather binds him to it. THE EDITOR, accordingly, KEEPS the privative ἀπροσδεής and treats the other as a slip. I have already pointed out similar [slips] in other not-good interpreters of Maximus: the dropping of one letter or syllable, by the easy lapse of a hasty scribe's hand, making [the passage] contradict Scripture openly, whereas the opposite is seriously noted by Maximus.

unplaced.anchorLine: καὶ ἀπροσδεὴς [male edita προσδεής] ὑπάρχων,
unplaced.en: PRIVATIVE BRACKET, p-0709: the printed text has ἀπροσδεής ('needing nothing'); the bracket says the earlier edition, badly edited, had προσδεής ('needing') without the alpha privative. So the bracket gives a VARIANT that LACKS the privative; the editor's own text keeps ἀ-. It is neither a supply nor a deletion by the editor: he restores ἀπροσδεής and calls προσδεής a misprint. Note (s) is about a different word.
